title: A foolish consistency
hook: a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds (Self-Reliance)

segments.voice: Yesterday, insist on yourself: a borrowed talent only half owned. Your line was never imitate. What did you do your own way, even clumsily? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

"But that's not what you said last year." It lands like a trap. Someone has dug up an old opinion of yours, a post, a remark at dinner, and set it next to what you think now. The two don't match. And the pull is to do one of two things: pretend you never really changed, or defend the old view just to look steady. Emerson saw that pull clearly, and in Self-Reliance he gave it a name in a line that gets quoted, sometimes with one important word left out. The missing word is the whole lesson.
screen: `THAT'S NOT WHAT YOU SAID.` → `THE PULL TO LOOK STEADY.` → `ONE WORD GETS LEFT OUT.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence, whole: "A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds, adored by little statesmen and philosophers and divines." The word that keeps getting dropped is foolish. Emerson isn't against consistency. Keeping a promise is consistent. Showing up for a friend year after year is consistent. He's against the foolish kind: sticking to a position only because you once said it. A hobgoblin, by the way, is a small mischievous spirit, the kind of thing that haunts a house. That's the picture: a petty little ghost that keeps a mind from moving. Second, why we do it. Emerson says we hold on to our past words because other people have nothing else to judge us by. They only have the record. So we start living for the record. Third, his remedy. He says to speak what you think now in plain, hard words, and tomorrow speak what tomorrow thinks, in hard words again, even if it contradicts everything you said today. Then he anticipates the objection: you'll be misunderstood. And he answers with a line of his own: "To be great is to be misunderstood." He names people misunderstood in their day, Socrates and Galileo among them. Fourth, what holds it together. Emerson trusts that a life lived honestly has a deeper shape than any one opinion. Seen from far enough off, he says, the zigzags of an honest life line up, the way a ship's tacking adds up to a course. Changing your mind isn't betraying yourself. Sometimes it's the faithful thing to do.
screen: `THE MISSING WORD: FOOLISH.` · `LIVING FOR THE RECORD.` · `SPEAK WHAT YOU THINK NOW.` · `THE ZIGZAG MAKES A COURSE.` · then, large: `A FOOLISH CONSISTENCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: change your mind on one thing. Settle, and breathe. Look for an opinion you've been carrying mostly out of habit. About a person, a food, a place, a kind of music, a way of doing things. Something you decided once and haven't looked at since. Turn it over now, honestly. What do you actually think today? If it's the same, fine. If it isn't, let it change, right here, without any explaining to anyone. Notice what that's like. The bell holds the time.
A foolish consistency. Emerson's hobgoblin of little minds: sticking to what you once said only because you said it. The key word is foolish. Today's word.
Your line: allowed to change. Today, if it fits, tell one person, simply and without apology, about something you see differently now. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

screen: `DAY 1196 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NOTHING CAN BRING YOU PEACE.`

howItsDone: Some readers use Emerson's line about a foolish consistency to make room for honest changes of mind, while keeping the steady kind of consistency that keeps promises and friendships.

notes: Confirm exact wording of both quotations against the 1841 text.

The 'speak what you think now in hard words' passage, the reason (others have no other data for computing our orbit than our past acts), and the ship's zigzag of tacks are paraphrased. Emerson's image is that the voyage of the best ship is a zigzag line of many tacks, straightened out by distance; the script gives no number.
Emerson's list of the misunderstood includes Pythagoras, Socrates, Jesus, Luther, Copernicus, Galileo and Newton; the script names only Socrates and Galileo.
'Hobgoblin' defined as a small mischievous spirit is a standard dictionary sense; no etymology given.
The hook says people quote the line 'often, and often' without 'foolish': a general observation, not a sourced count.
Editor: cut the unsourced frequency claim ('people quote it often, and often') to 'sometimes'; the practice no longer tells the listener the change feels light; 'readers often' to 'some readers'.
